speaker: astra
usageNotes: Use after identification, not as the label for an unresolved contact.
These are catalogue facts; none requires a crater, plume, ocean or atmosphere to be resolved by the current renderer.
The lines are independent of observer distance and route progress. Add arrival, receding, braking or missed-approach dialogue only from measured telemetry.
Do not turn these discoveries into a required checklist. Optional navigation sentences offer a bearing or permission to linger.
Hyperion's chaotic rotation is a real-world fact, not a claim that the frozen snapshot simulates its tumble.
Avoid the older Mimas page's frozen-solid interior claim; newer research questions it. The large Herschel crater is the stable fact used here.
Source URLs are for Flight notes or research credits; they need not appear in the subtitle itself. All subtitle wording is original.
Europa’s port and travel history are fictional worldbuilding performed by Astra, not present-day scientific claims. The fact field and citation describe the real moon separately.

Mimas.text: that's Mimas, with the enormous Herschel impact crater. let's give it a little more room than the last visitor did.
Mimas.fact: Herschel crater spans roughly one third of Mimas's diameter.

Enceladus.text: Enceladus has an ocean beneath its ice. and jets that carry some of it into space. we can linger longer if you'd like.
Enceladus.fact: Enceladus has a subsurface global saltwater ocean that supplies water-vapour and ice jets.

Tethys.text: Tethys has a crater called Odysseus. and a great valley called Ithaca. someone else was thinking about a way home.
Tethys.fact: Odysseus is a large impact crater; Ithaca Chasma is an approximately 2,000 km valley.

Dione.text: Dione's pale streaks turned out to be cliffs of exposed ice. i'll keep its bearing while you choose our next move.
Dione.fact: Cassini resolved the previously described wispy terrain into bright ice walls and fracture cliffs.

Rhea.text: Rhea is Saturn's second largest moon. with an ancient surface crowded with craters. a turbulent marriage, perhaps.
Rhea.fact: Rhea is Saturn's second-largest moon and has heavily cratered, old icy terrain.

Titan.text: Titan has weather, rivers, and lakes beneath that haze. although the lakes are methane and ethane. familiar ideas, rather different arrangements.
Titan.fact: Titan has a substantial hazy atmosphere and surface rivers, lakes and seas of liquid hydrocarbons.

Hyperion.text: Hyperion is full of deep craters. and its rotation tumbles unpredictably. we don't have to take navigational advice from it.
Hyperion.fact: Hyperion is irregular, deeply cratered and rotates chaotically.

Iapetus.text: Iapetus has a dark hemisphere, a bright one. and a mountain ridge along its middle. even out here, a world can be quite particular about its appearance.
Iapetus.fact: Iapetus has strongly contrasting hemispheres and a prominent equatorial mountain ridge.

Io.text: Io has hundreds of volcanoes. Jupiter's pull helps keep its interior hot. she's wandered far enough. let's make this a gentle visit.
Io.fact: Io is highly volcanically active; tidal forcing involving Jupiter and neighboring moons heats its interior.

Europa.text: Europa. its subsurface oceans have made it an ideal port for travel in and out of the solar system. we would've exited here, had you not dismissed my fuel warnings.
Europa.fact: Europa's icy surface is fractured, and strong evidence supports an underlying saltwater ocean.

Ganymede.text: Ganymede is the largest moon in the system. it generates its own magnetic field. a rather substantial landmark.
Ganymede.fact: Ganymede is the solar system's largest moon and the only moon known to generate its own magnetic field.

Callisto.text: Callisto has kept scars of impact for billions of years. our little flyby needn't add to the collection.
Callisto.fact: Callisto's ancient rocky and icy surface is heavily cratered and has undergone little resurfacing.

Gaspra.text: that's Gaspra, a cratered little asteroid that turns once in about seven hours. small enough to miss if we hurry.
Gaspra.fact: Galileo images show numerous craters; Gaspra's rotation period is just over seven hours.

Mars.text: that's Mars, iron rusting in the dust, god of war. let's keep this visit peaceful, unlike last time.
Mars.fact: Oxidized iron in rocks and dust gives Mars its reddish appearance.

Earth.text: we found Earth. oceans. oxygen. every fire, every crossing, every road you know. it's time to go home.
Earth.fact: Earth has stable liquid-water oceans on its surface.

Venus.text: that's Venus, beneath the clouds of sulfuric acid. we'll light her lamp when we get home.
Venus.fact: Venus's dense atmosphere contains sulfuric-acid clouds.
